name: client-server
context: Distributed systems where clients initiate requests and servers provide responses over a network. The client-server pattern is the foundational architecture for networked applications: a client sends requests to a server, which processes those requests and returns results. The server is a resource provider; the client is a resource consumer. This pattern underlies virtually all web applications, APIs, and networked services. Its enduring dominance stems from its simplicity, scalability through stateless server design, and broad tooling ecosystem. While often considered 'basic', the decisions made within a client-server architecture — around state management, authentication, caching, and error handling — determine the reliability and performance of the entire system.
benefits: Centralized resource management: shared data and business logic live on the server, ensuring consistency
Scalability: servers can be replicated and load-balanced; clients are lightweight and stateless
Security: sensitive business logic and data remain on the server, not distributed to client devices
Heterogeneous clients: a single server can serve many different client types (web, mobile, API)
Ease of update: server-side changes take effect immediately without needing to deploy client updates
Simple conceptual model: developers immediately understand request-response semantics
Broad tooling and protocol ecosystem: HTTP, REST, gRPC, WebSocket all implement this pattern
tradeoffs: Network dependency: both client and server must be available; network partitions cause failures
Latency: every operation incurs at minimum one network round-trip
Server as single point of failure: without replication, server outages take down all clients
Stateful server complexity: maintaining session state on the server creates memory pressure and replication challenges
Overfetching and underfetching: REST endpoints often return too much or too little data for the client's needs
Synchronous request-response: not suited for real-time, push-based, or event-driven interactions without additional mechanisms
Client device limitations: clients on constrained devices may not handle large payloads or complex response parsing efficiently
use_cases: A web application where browsers request HTML pages and API data from a central server
A mobile banking app where the client communicates with backend financial services via REST or gRPC
An internal tool where a lightweight client connects to a centralized server providing business logic
A third-party integration where partners consume a company's data through a versioned REST API
avoid_when: Sub-millisecond latency is required and caching cannot adequately mask network round-trips
The system must operate offline or with intermittent connectivity
Real-time updates need to be pushed from server to client without polling
Highly concurrent, stateful workloads where the overhead of request-response per operation is prohibitive
Collaborative editing where optimistic UI with local state conflicts with a server-centric model
component_types: Client: Initiates requests to the server; handles user interface, local state, and result presentation
Server: Receives requests, applies business logic, manages data, and returns responses
Network: The transport medium (HTTP, TLS, WebSocket); its characteristics constrain the interaction patterns available
Load Balancer: Distributes client requests across multiple server instances for scalability and availability
Cache: Optional intermediate store between client and server, reducing repeated requests for unchanged data
API Gateway: Entry point on the server side that handles authentication, rate limiting, and request routing
Session Store: Optional server-side state repository for maintaining user sessions across requests
anti_patterns: Stovepipe Integration: each client creates its own server protocol, leading to N×M integration complexity
Chatty API: client makes many small requests instead of batching, causing excessive network round-trips
God Server: the server becomes a monolithic application handling every concern from business logic to email delivery to report generation
Credential Leakage: sensitive credentials embedded in client code or logged on the server
Stateless Protocol, Stateful Application Done Wrong: treating HTTP as if it maintains session state without proper session management
Missing Caching: every request hits the server even for data that rarely changes, causing unnecessary load
design_principles: Stateless Server: each request contains all information needed to process it; servers hold no client context between requests
Layered Server Internals: server-side code follows its own internal layering (presentation, business logic, data access)
Cache Wisely: identify which responses are cacheable and at what granularity; leverage CDN and browser caching
Fail Fast on Invalid Input: validate client input at the server boundary before processing; never trust the client
Separate Concerns at the API Layer: authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and business logic are handled at distinct layers
Version APIs from Day One: even internal APIs benefit from versioning from initial release to prevent breaking changes
Design for Evolution: prefer hypermedia and well-documented contracts over rigid point-to-point integrations
best_practices: Use Stateless Authentication: JWTs or signed tokens rather than server-side sessions to avoid memory pressure and replication complexity
Implement Proper Error Handling: machine-readable error codes plus human-readable messages; distinguish client errors (4xx) from server errors (5xx)
Apply Rate Limiting: protect the server from abuse; use standard headers like X-RateLimit-Remaining
Log at the Right Level: log request IDs consistently across client and server to enable distributed tracing
Choose the Right Protocol: HTTP/REST for request-response; WebSocket for real-time bidirectional; gRPC for high-performance internal communication
Cache Aggressively at Appropriate Layers: CDN for static assets, Redis for frequently read data, HTTP cache headers for client-side caching
Design for Backward Compatibility: add fields to responses rather than removing them; version before breaking changes
